cues.text: The Jewish Revolt
Tension between Jewish Judea and Roman rule had simmered for decades under a series of often corrupt procurators.

In AD 66, following provocations by the procurator Gessius Florus — including the seizure of silver from the Temple treasury and a massacre of Jerusalem's residents — open revolt broke out across Judea.
An early Roman force under Cestius Gallus was driven back from Jerusalem with heavy losses, emboldening the rebellion.
Emperor Nero dispatched the general Vespasian , with his son Titus , to suppress the revolt.
Vespasian methodically subdued Galilee and the surrounding countryside.
The campaign was interrupted by political chaos in Rome following Nero's death in 68.
Vespasian himself was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 69, leaving Titus to complete the siege of Jerusalem.
The Siege of Jerusalem
Titus brought his legions before the walls of Jerusalem in the spring of AD 70, during the Passover season, when the city was swollen with pilgrims.

The siege lasted roughly five months, marked by severe famine within the walls, factional fighting among rival Jewish defenders, and repeated Roman assaults on the city's successive lines of fortification.
Jesus had foretold the city's destruction decades earlier, a prophecy Christian writers of the following generation would frequently recall as the siege ground toward its conclusion.
The Burning of the Temple
In late August or early September, Roman forces breached the Temple precincts.
According to the Jewish historian Josephus, Titus wished to preserve the Temple as an ornament of Roman victory.
However, in the chaos of the final fighting, a soldier threw a firebrand into the building, and it was consumed by flames despite efforts to stop the blaze.
With the Temple destroyed, the daily sacrifices that had defined Jewish worship since the time of Solomon's Temple came to an end.

The Romans went on to raze most of the rest of the city; only a portion of its western retaining wall — venerated today as the Western Wall — and three great towers of Herod's palace were left standing.
Consequences for Jews and Christians
The destruction of the Temple in AD 70 marked the effective end of Second Temple Judaism and, alongside it, of the Temple-centered priesthood and sacrificial system.

It accelerated the emergence of rabbinic Judaism, centered on synagogue and Torah rather than Temple sacrifice, and hardened the separation between the young Christian Church and the Jewish community from which it had grown.
For Christian writers, the fall of Jerusalem was widely read as confirmation of Christ’s own prophecy in the Gospels.
This prophecy, recorded, for instance, in Luke 21 and Matthew 24, stated that not one stone of the Temple would be left upon another.

Titus later celebrated his victory with a triumph in Rome, commemorated by the Arch of Titus, still standing in the Roman Forum, whose relief carvings depict soldiers carrying off the Temple's golden menorah and other sacred vessels.
